atoms.text: The Great Barrier Reef is the world's largest coral reef system. It consists of 2,900 individual reefs and about 900 islands. This special ecosystem stretches for over 2,300 km and covers more than the size of Italy. It is located off the coast of Queensland in the north-east of Australia in the Coral Sea. The tropical climate enables the existence of large amounts of stony and soft-corals.

atoms.text: Corals aren't plants as it may seem at first. Actually, they are made of colonies of many tiny animal organisms called coral polyps. Since they have a need for sunlight but can't grow above sea level, corals can only be found in water up to a depth of 150 metres. The Great Barrier Reef is home to 600 different coral species, which create a convenient environment for other species. About 1,500 fish species inhabit the reef as well as dolphins, sharks, whales, sea snakes, sea turtles and seahorses.

atoms.a: Why can corals not grow below 150 metres in the water?
b: They can't breathe below that depth.

atoms.text: The Great Barrier Reef has been threatened for several centuries. More recently, climate change has caused higher water temperatures and poor water quality which pose an enormous threat to this sensitive ecosystem. Additionally, overfishing and pollution stress the wellbeing of the reef. A natural threat is the coral eating crown-of-thorns starfish. During an outbreak the starfish can destroy up to 90% of the corals in the area.

atoms.text: Due to several causes, like rising water temperatures, corals can lose their colour and become white. This phenomenon is called coral bleaching. Corals normally have a symbiotic relationship with microscopic algae feeding the corals and giving them their colour. However, if the coral is stressed because of a changing environment, the algae leave. In the end, the coral is left bleached and vulnerable.
